accommodate

/uh-KOM-uh-dayt/ — spelling hook: it's roomy enough for two c's AND two m's · verb

Hear It

What It Means

To accommodate is to adjust or make room in order to fit someone's needs or wishes.

The airline agreed to accommodate the stranded passengers by booking them on the next flight at no charge.

Example

Two guests told the innkeeper they couldn't climb stairs, another needed a gluten-free breakfast, and a third asked for a late checkout. By evening she had accommodated every request, rearranging the rooms, revising the menu, and adjusting the schedule so everyone got what they needed.

To merely 'tolerate' guests is to put up with them; to accommodate them, as the innkeeper did, is to actively adjust your own plans to fit their needs and wishes.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

oblige: To oblige someone is to do a favor or grant a request — a one-time kindness that costs little. To accommodate is to go further and adjust your own plans, space, or schedule so another person's needs fit. Obliging is a single act; accommodating is a rearrangement.

adapt: To adapt is to adjust something to suit new conditions — a recipe, a plan, an organism. To accommodate is to make that adjustment for a person, bending your own arrangements so someone else's needs and wishes fit. You adapt to circumstances; you accommodate people.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

refuse: to say no to a request

hinder: to make things harder for someone

Where it sits · how far you bend for others — allow → accommodate → indulge

allow vs. accommodate: Allow is weaker than accommodate — allowing something just means not blocking it, while accommodating means actively adjusting your own plans to make it work.

indulge vs. accommodate: Indulge is stronger than accommodate — accommodating meets reasonable needs, but indulging gives in to every wish, even unreasonable ones.

Build the Word

The pieces

prefix — ac-

prefix — ac-: to, toward (variant of Latin ad-)

prefix — com-

prefix — com-: together, fully (Latin)

root — mod

root — mod: measure, manner (from Latin modus)

suffix — -ate

suffix — -ate: to make (verb-forming) (Latin)

Put it together

Put it together: Accommodate stacks ac- ('to, toward') onto Latin commodus ('fitting, suitable') — com- ('together') + modus ('measure') — plus -ate ('to make'). To accommodate is literally 'to make fit to' someone: adjusting things to their measure.

Use the root in a new word: modify

Use the root in a new word: modify: Engineers modified the bridge design after the safety review.
